list.listitem: The cause of hypoglycemia can usually be identified on the basis of history, with a focus on medications and the circumstances surrounding episodes. C
Obtain a glucose measurement at the time of symptoms. Biochemical hypoglycemia must be documented to prevent the mislabeling of healthy individuals. C
The oral glucose tolerance test is not useful. C
Measure pancreatic hormones, counter-regulatory hormones, and ketones in a hypoglycemic specimen, if ordered. C
Although rare, insulinoma is the most common cause of endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.

background.definition: Hypoglycemia is the presence of low blood glucose, typically below 70 mg/dL, generally in the presence of symptoms.

list.listitem: Diabetes mellitus (DM): common, especially Type 1.

In a Australian follow-up study of over 11,000 patients with type 2 DM assigned to either intensive or standard glucose control, at least one episode of hypoglycemia occurred in 2.1% (231 patients); 150 in the intensive glucose control (2.7% of 5571 patients) and 81 in the standard glucose control group (1.5% of 5569 patients).
Others: uncommon to rare.

In an Australian follow-up study of over 11,000 patients with type 2 DM, severe hypoglycemia was associated with a significant increase in the adjusted risks of major macrovascular events (hazard ratio (HR) 2.88; 95% CI, 2.01-4.12), major microvascular events (HR 1.81; 95% CI, 1.19-2.74), cardiovascular mortality (HR 2.68; 95% CI, 1.72-4.19), and all-cause mortality (HR 2.69; 95% CI, 1.97-3.67).
In critically ill patients in the ICU, moderate to severe hypoglycemia is associated with an increased risk of death.
A comprehensive list of causes is shown in .
The most common cause of hypoglycemia is iatrogenic from medications for diabetes. Intensive control of diabetes doubles the risk of hypoglycemia compared to less intense control.

Some medications to treat diabetes are more likely to cause hypoglycemia than others. For example, patients are more likely to get hypoglycemic with glimepiride than linagliptin. (NNH = 3-4 for at least one episode.)
Measures to improve glycemic control will increase the risk of severe hypoglycemic reactions in frail elderly.
A variety of nondiabetic medications are also associated with hypoglycemia.
Reactive hypoglycemia is often established by circumstances, and is more likely if the patient has had previous gastric surgery or uses alcohol.
Tight glycemic control leads to more hypoglycemia in patients in the pediatric ICU.
A validated tool may be useful to determine which patients with Type 1 diabetes have impaired awareness of hypoglycemia.

Use of basal bolus insulin in hospitalized patients compared to sliding scale insulin may minimize hypoglycemia. More research is needed on prevention of hypoglycemia in non-critically ill hospitalized patients.
There is no difference in severe or symptomatic hypoglycemic episodes in hospitalized patients comparing sliding scale insulin regimens and non- sliding scale insulin.
Real time continuous glucose monitoring decreases hypoglycemia in patients with Type 1 DM and lack of hypoglycemic awareness NNT = 4.

Factors associated with a higher rate of hospitalization for hypoglycemia among older people in care facilities include high or medium level of care needs, renal disease, prior hospitalization with hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, use of insulin, sulfonylureas, or angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.
Symptoms directly related to CNS effects are called neuroglycopenia.
Hypoglycemia can be divided into acute, subacute, and chronic.
Acute hypoglycemia: sweating, anxiety, tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, pallor, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias.
Subacute hypoglycemia: episodic disorientation, somnolence, personality changes, amnesia, loss of consciousness.
Chronic hypoglycemia: progressive mental illness resembling personality disorders, schizophrenia, paranoid psychosis, depression, dementia.
Collect capillary blood sample while symptomatic (a venous sample may give false positive results).
Provocation can be attempted with fasting (with or without exercise) or with a carbohydrate-rich mixed meal.
Glucose tolerance testing is associated with high rate of false positives and is not recommended.

If hypoglycemia is suspected, include plasma insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, ketones, and growth hormone testing (see algorithm in ). In one systematic review of sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia, average plasma insulin level was ≥3.9 muIU/mL and C-peptide was ≥1.4 ng/mL.
See the diagnostic algorithm in .
Most patients do not benefit from an extensive biochemical evaluation.

feature.caption: Causes of Hypoglycemia.
feature.feature_body:
Diabetes treatment
Nondiabetic medications (eg, quinolones, salicylates, beta-blockers, haloperidol, disopyramide, quinine)
Reactive (excludes fasting hypoglycemia) Idiopathic Postgastric surgery Alcohol-induced Noninsulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglycemia
Pancreatic Insulinoma, including multiple endocrine neoplasia 1 Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglycemia Nesidioblastosis Pluriglandular syndrome
Nonislet cell tumors Insulin-like growth factor secreting tumors Lymphoma, myeloma, leukemia Metastatic cancer
Organ failure Advanced liver disease End-stage renal disease, dialysis Heart failure Acute respiratory failure
Endocrine disease Hypopituitarism and hypothalamic insufficiency Adrenal failure and cortisol resistance Hypothyroidism Postoperative removal of pheochromocytoma
Inborn errors of metabolism Glycogen storage disease Galactosemia Hereditary fructose intolerance Carnitine deficiency Disorders of gluconeogenesis Disorders of mitochondrial B oxidation
Autoimmune AIS Anti-insulin receptor Pancreatic Graves' disease
Miscellaneous Sepsis Starvation, including anorexia nervosa Total parenteral nutrition Severe exercise Unripe ackee nuts Mushrooms causing acute liver failure Alcohol toxicity
